var_label: Average daily PM2.5 concentration from monitors
var_def: The arithmetic mean of PM2.5 measurements for all monitors within the geographic unit. All days during the time span where data is available are included in the dataset. If PM2.5 data is not available for a particular day, then the PM2.5 mean are missing values.

var_label: Standard Deviation of daily PM2.5 concentration from monitors
var_def: Standard deviation of PM2.5 measurements for all monitors within the geographic unit. All days during the time span where data is available are included in the dataset. If PM2.5 data is not available for a particular day, then the PM2.5 standard deviation are missing values. A higher value indictates more variability in the PM2.5 measures used to calculated the mean and median values.

Number of monitors used to calculate daily PM2.5 average and variance measures for the geographic unit. All days during the time span where data is available are included in the dataset. If PM2.5 data is not available for a particular day, then the PM2.5 number of monitors are missing values. A higher number indicates more monitors were used to calculate the PM2.5 metrics.

Total number of collisions, this is the count of all the collisions that occurred in the month.
Total number of collisions that occurred on weekends. Weekends extend from Friday to Sunday.
Total number of people who died because of a collision that occurred in the month.

var_label: Total number of collisions with alcohol involvement
var_def: Total number of collisions where alcohol had involvement, the alcohol use was detected for the responsible driver via a breathalyzer test. The breathalyzer used by police in Mexico indicates alcohol was detected or not and does not indicate the blood alcohol level. It is a screening tool to obtain a legal blood draw test of blood alcohol content.

var_label: Total number of weekend collisions with alcohol involvement
var_def: Total number of collisions where alcohol had involvement on the weekend, the alcohol use was detected for the responsible driver via a breathalyzer test. The breathalyzer used by police in Mexico indicates alcohol was detected or not and does not indicate the blood alcohol level. It is a screening tool to obtain a legal blood draw test of blood alcohol content. Weekends extend from Friday to Sunday.
Total number of people that resulted injured because of a collision.
Total number of fatal collisions, this is the total count where a person died due to a collision.

var_label: Total number of fatal weekend collisions
var_def: Total number of fatal collisions, this is the total count where a person died due to a collision. Weekends extend from Friday to Sunday.

var_label: Total number of collisions with injured person (without deaths)
var_def: Total number of collisions that had at least one injured person excluding collisions in which a death occurred, this variable excludes collisions that had at least one person die.

var_label: Total number of collisions that had at least one injured person
var_def: Total number of collisions that had at least one injured person regardless of whether a death occurred. This variable includes collisions with injuries and deaths, and collisions with injuries but without deaths.

var_label: Total number of weekend collisions with injured person (without deaths)
var_def: Total number of collisions that had at least one injured person excluding collisions in which a death occurred, this variable excludes collisions that had at least one person die. Weekends extend from Friday to Sunday.

var_label: Total number of weekend collisions that had at least one injured person
var_def: Total number of collisions that had at least one injured person regardless of whether a death occurred. This variable includes collisions with injuries and deaths, and collisions with injuries but without deaths. Weekends extend from Friday to Sunday.

Average of the airline distance from L3 centroids to the nearest park for all the L3 units that are nested within the L1/L2.  Interpretation: Higher values indicate greater distance (or - lower proximity), on average, to urban parks at the neighborhood (L3) level within L1/L2 units.

var_label: Average route distance to the nearest park
var_def: Average of the street route distance from L3 centroid to the nearest park in meters for all the L3 units that are nested within the L1/L2. Interpretation: Higher values indicate greater distance (or - lower proximity) to parks.

The airline distance from L3 centroid to the nearest large park (as calculated from the nearest vertex of the large park). This variable is available only at L3 and it currently includes only parks that are defined as large according to country based tertiles. For L3 units with a park located 20km or more the distance to the nearest park variable was labeled NA (Not applicable). Interpretation: Higher values indicate greater distance (or - lower proximity) to large urban parks.

Number of large parks that fall within a unit. Any large park that fall within the unit's boundaries will be counted, even if only part of the large park is in the unit. This metric currently includes only parks that are defined as large according to country based tertiles. Interpretation: Higher values indicate higher prevalence of large urban parks.

var_label: Number of large parks per capita
var_def: Number of parks that fall within the unit (total number of large parks that fall within the unit's boundaries, even if only part of the large park is in the unit) divided by the total population (2017) within the administrative boundary and then multiplied by 1,000. This metric currently includes only parks that are defined as large according to country based tertiles. Interpretation: Higher values indicate more large parks per capita.

The percentage of parks that are large-sized. [(“Number of large urban parks”/”Number of urban parks”)*100]. This metric currently includes only parks that are defined as large according to country based tertiles. Interpretation: Higher values suggest that large parks comprise higher percentages of all urban parks.

var_label: Route distance to nearest large park
var_def: Distance by street route from L3 centroid to the nearest large park (as calculated from the nearest vertex of the park). This variable is available only at L3 and it currently includes only parks that are defined as large according to country based tertiles. Interpretation: Higher values indicate greater distance (or - lower proximity) to urban parks. For L3 units with a park located 20km or more the distance to the nearest large park variable was labeled NA (Not applicable).

Median of the airline distance from L3 centroids to the nearest park for all the L3 units that are nested within the L1/L2.  Interpretation: Higher values indicate greater distance (or - lower proximity), on average, to urban parks at the neighborhood (L3) level within L1/L2 units.

The airline distance from L3 centroid to the nearest medium park (as calculated from the nearest vertex of the  medium park). var_label: Number of medium parks per capita

The percentage of all parks that are medium-sized. [(“Number of medium urban parks”/”Number of urban parks”)*100]. The airline distance from L3 centroid to the nearest park (as calculated from the nearest vertex of the park). This variable is available only at L3. Interpretation: Higher values indicate greater distance (or - lower proximity) to urban parks.

Number of parks that fall within the unit (total number of parks that fall within the unit's boundaries, even if only part of the park is in the unit ) divided by the total population within the administrative boundary and then multiplied by 1,000. Sum of the area of all parks that fall within the geographic unit. If a park crosses the boundary of the unit, only the area within the unit is counted. Interpretation: Higher values indicate more area covered by urban parks.

var_label: Urban average travel time in traffic
var_def: Measures the average travel time in congestion. Larger values mean longer average travel times in the street network (minutes). The index for each area unit is approximated by measuring delays for 30 random origin-destination pairs in the street network and seven points in time during peak hours of a typical weekday. Each pair of points and moment in time determine a set of observations for each unit. The index for each area unit is approximated by measuring delays for 30 random origin-destination pairs in the street network and seven points in time during peak hours of a typical weekday. Each pair of points and moment in time determine a set of observations for each unit. Year of data: January 2018.

Measures the increase in travel times due to congestion in the street network. The index for each area unit is approximated by measuring delays for 30 random origin-destination pairs in the street network and seven points in time during peak hours of a typical weekday. Each pair of points and moment in time determine a set of observations for each unit. Interpretation: Index ranges from zero to infinity. A value of zero means that traffic does not increase travel time. An index of X means travel time in traffic is (1+X) times the travel time without traffic. Year of data: January 2018.

Measures the average travel time delay (in minutes) due to congestion in the street network. Larger values mean longer time delays due to congestion (minutes). The index for each area unit is approximated by measuring delays for 30 random origin-destination pairs in the street network and seven points in time during peak hours of a typical weekday. Each pair of points and moment in time determine a set of observations for each unit. Area in km2 of the administrative boundary. This is the total area, including land and water, within L3's boundary.

Measures the average ratio of network distances to straight-line distances. Average of the length of each edge divided by the great circle distances between the nodes of each edge.  Interpretation: For each edge in the network, its circuity is the ratio between the edge length and the straight line distance between its two end points. Varies from 1 to infinity, where streets that are straight lines have circuity of 1, and curved streets have higher circuity. Year of data: September 2017 for L1, January 2018 for L2

Each intersection (a point where more than 2 streets meet) becomes a node of the network. Total number of intersections measures the number of nodes with more than one street emanating from them (thus excluding dead-ends). Year of data: September 2017 for L1_AD, January 2018 for L2, 2020 for L3.

Measures the amount of intersections per km2 of area. Each intersection (a point where more than 2 streets meet) becomes a node of the network. Node density of the set of nodes with more than one street emanating from them (thus excluding dead-ends). Higher values means more connected. Interpretation: Varies from 0 to infinity. Cities with higher values have a lot of intersections by unit of area. Year of data: September 2017 for L1_AD, January 2018 for L2, 2020 for L3.

Measures the amount of intersections where exactly 3 streets meet per km2 of area. Each intersection (a point where more than 2 streets meet) becomes a node of the network. Node density of the set of nodes with 3 streets emanating from them. Higher values means more connected. Interpretation: Varies from 0 to infinity. Cities with higher values have a lot of intersections with 3 incoming streets by unit of area.Year of data: September 2017 for L1_AD, January 2018 for L2

Measures the amount of intersections where exactly 4 streets meet per km2 of area. Each intersection (a point where more than 2 streets meet) becomes a node of the network. Node density of the set of nodes with 4 streets emanating from them. Higher values means more connected. Interpretation: Varies from 0 to infinity. Cities with higher values have a lot of intersections with 4 incoming streets by unit of area.Year of data: September 2017 for L1_AD, January 2018 for L2

Measures the total length of streets in meters with four or more lanes per km2 of area. Interpretation: Varies from 0 to infinity. Cities with higher values have more large streets per unit of area; Higher values means more traffic, more obstacles, less walkability. Year of data: September 2017 for L1_AD, January 2018 for L2.

Measures the total length of streets in meters per km2 of area. Each intersection (a point where more than 2 streets meet) becomes a node of the network and each street segment connecting two intersections becomes an edge in the network. Street density sums of all links in the undirected representation of the network divided by the area. Interpretation: Varies from 0 to infinity. Cities with higher values have a lot of streets by unit of area. Year of data:  September 2017 for L1_AD, January 2018 for L2, 2020 for L3.

Measures the average length of streets in the street network. Each intersection (a point where more than 2 streets meet) becomes a node of the network and each street segment connecting two intersections becomes an edge in the network. Interpretation: Small values represent smaller blocks and large values represent larger street segments or blocks. Year of data: September 2017 for L1_AD, January 2018 for L2.

Measures the distribution of the number of streets that meet at each intersection of the street network. Each intersection (a point where more than 2 streets meet) becomes a node of the network and each street segment connecting two intersections becomes an edge in the network. Interpretation: Varies from 2 to infinity. Higher values mean on average intersections connect to more intersections. Year of data: September 2017 for L1_AD, January 2018 for L2.

Measures the distribution of the number of streets that meet at each intersection of the street network.  Each intersection (a point where more than 2 streets meet) becomes a node of the network and each street segment connecting two intersections becomes an edge in the network. The standard deviation of the number of physical streets (i.e., edges in the undirected representation of the graph) that emanate from each intersection and dead-end. Interpretation: Higher values mean more variability in the number of incoming edges (streets) for each node in the network; the statistical and spatial distributions of number of streets per intersection characterize the type, prevalence, and dispersion of intersection connectedness in the network. Year of data: September 2017 for L1_AD, January 2018 for L2.

Total street length considering all types of streets within the areal unit. Each intersection (a point where more than 2 streets meet) becomes a node of the network and each street segment connecting two intersections becomes an edge in the network. Street length sums of all links in the undirected representation of the network. Year of data: September 2017 for L1_AD, January 2018 for L2, 2020 for L3.
An indicator variable for sources of L3 boundary

Measure of the Aerial Tram system supply. The aerial tramway is based on the principle of cableways in sightseeing tours in alpine resorts. The aerial tramway is a type or aerial lift which uses one or two stationary support ropes and a third moving rope to move a cabin through a defined path. For the cities where it does not exist, we assume zero as the value of the city. Interpretation: The total length in km of Aerial Tram. A unit with higher values has a bigger aerial tram system. Country team input: The draft of measures was sent to each country team to check for face validity.  Country teams used their expert knowledge and/or any existing criteria used to suggest any changes to the aerial tram variables at L1 and L2 “subcity”.  Year of data: December 2017

Total urban area (in hectares) divided by number of urban patches. Interpretation: Indicator of urban fragmentation. Larger values reflect a larger size of urban development; low values reflect scattered, small development.

Weighted average of urban patch size (in hectares). This value is weighted by the area of each patch. By weighting by patch size, larger urban patches have a higher influence in this weighted-average metric. Researchers could decide at their own discretion on using this weighted index or the corresponding unweighted one. Interpretation: Indicator of fragmentation. Larger values reflect a larger size of urban development; low values reflect scattered, small development.

Total perimeter of all patches multiplied by the corresponding area weight, and divided by the total area of the geographic unit. This is the area-weighted version of edge density. By weighting by patch size, larger urban patches have a higher influence in this weighted-average metric. Researchers could decide at their own discretion on using this weighted index or the corresponding unweighted one. Interpretation: Indicator of fragmentation and shape complexity. A higher value indicates, for the same total area of urban patches: (1) there are likely to be more smaller patches versus fewer larger patches, and (2) on average, patches have a more complex shape.

Mean distance (in meters) to the nearest urban patch within the geographic boundary. This value is weighted by the area of each patch. Interpretation: Indicator of isolation among patches of a similar class, a higher value indicates higher level of isolation. By weighting by patch size, larger urban patches have a higher influence in this weighted-average metric.

Shape index is a ratio of the actual perimeter of a patch to the minimum perimeter possible for a maximally compact patch with the same size. The area-weighted mean shape index is the weighted average of the shape index for each patch within the geographic boundary. This index is weighted by the area of each patch. Interpretation: Shape index ranges from 1 to infinity, with 1 being the index for a patch that is maximally compact. A lower value indicates higher levels of compactness of each individual patch. By weighting by patch size, larger urban patches have a higher influence in this weighted-average metric.

Measure of overall levels of Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) supply. For cities where there is no BRT system we assign zero as the value of the geographic level. The BRT is a bus-based public transport system designed to improve upon the capacity and reliability of a conventional bus system. A BRT system includes roadways specially designated as corridors for buses and stations for boarding. BRT aims to combine the capacity and speed of a metro and the flexibility and lower cost of a bus system. The total length in km of BRT in the geographic unit. A unit with higher values have a bigger BRT system. Year of data: September 2017. Country team input: The draft of measures was sent to each country team to check for face validity.  Country teams used their expert knowledge and/or any existing criteria used to suggest any changes to the BRT variables at L1 and L_2 “subcity”.

One-way Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) fare in USD. The BRT price trip standard in USD.  The BRT is a bus-based public transport system designed to improve upon the capacity and reliability of a conventional bus system. A BRT system includes roadways specially designated as corridors for buses and stations for boarding. BRT aims to combine the capacity and speed of a metro and the flexibility and lower cost of a bus system. A unit with a higher travel price indicates a higher cost for the user per trip. Year of data: September 2017

Measure of bicycle lane system supply.  Bicycle facilities: public infrastructure and other areas aimed at the exclusive or shared use of bicycles. This can be an exclusive lane of a public road or an independent way where bicycles can transit. Interpretation: The total length in km of bicycle lane. A unit with higher values has more and larger bicycle lanes. Country team input: The draft of measures was sent to each country team to check for face validity.  Country teams used their expert knowledge and/or any existing criteria used to suggest any changes to the bicycle lanes variables at L and L2 “subcity”. In a preliminary audit, we modified the values according to the information of the experts in the countries and the information collected from OpenStreetMap. For each city with a value different from zero or missing, we take the highest value between the value from the official source and OpenStreetMap. Year of data: December 2017

Foundation year for cities at Level 1 (Applicable only to L1AD and L1UX units). Interpretation: Colonial foundation of the city. Earliest date of colonial settlement is used as foundation year when official date was not available or when discrepancies were found between data sources. City foundation years range from 1502 to 1992.

Binary indicator that distinguishes between coastal (with a value of 1) and inland geographies (with a value of 0). Coastal geographies are those with parts of their boundaries within 1 km from the closest coastline, whereas inland regions represent the rest. Interpretation: Coastal regions should be treated differently as they are more influenced by oceans.

var_label: Coefficient of variation of the urban patch size
var_def: The standard deviation of the patch size within the geographic boundary, divided by the mean patch size within the geographic boundary. Interpretation: A higher value indicates a higher level of variation of patch sizes; a lower value indicates a more even distribution of patch sizes

Major climate zone in a geography, indicating its seasonal precipitation and temperature patterns. Interpretation: Representative climate patterns of seasonal precipitation and temperature patterns in a geography. These patterns control for background difference in climate (precipitation and temperature) and biophysical environment (e.g., availability of greenspace and blue space).

Measure level of demand of the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system.  The BRT is a bus-based public transport system designed to improve upon the capacity and reliability of a conventional bus system. A BRT system includes roadways specially designated as corridors for buses and stations for boarding. BRT aims to combine the capacity and speed of a metro and the flexibility and lower cost of a bus system. Interpretation: It is calculated as the ratio between number of users of BRT and total population (applicable only to L1). A unit with higher BRT demand values indicates a system with higher level of demand. Year of data: September 2017.

Total perimeter of all urban patches, divided by the total area of the geographic unit measured in meters per hectare. Interpretation: Indicator of fragmentation and shape complexity. A higher value indicates, for the same total area of urban patches: (1) on average, there are likely to be more smaller patches, versus fewer larger patches, and (2) on average, patches have more complex shapes.

The sum of squares of urban patch size, divided by the total area of the geographic unit in hectare. Interpretation: Indicator of fragmentation where larger patches have higher weights. Larger values reflect a larger size of urban development; low values reflect scattered, small development.
Average elevation over land area (excluding water) in meters. Large value reflects more hilliness.
Maximum elevation over land area (excluding water) in meters. Large value reflects more hilliness.
Median elevation over land area (excluding water) in meters. Large value reflects more hilliness.
Minimum elevation over land area (excluding water) in meters. Large value reflects more hilliness.
25th percentile of elevation over land area (excluding water) in meters. Large value reflects more hilliness or more variations in hilliness.
75th percentile of elevation over land area (excluding water) in meters. Large value reflects more hilliness or more variations in hilliness.
Standard deviation of elevation over land area (excluding water) in meters. Large value reflects more variation in hilliness.

var_label: Differences between worldpop- and census-based population
var_def: Worldpop estimated population minus census-based population then divided by the census-based population. Interpretation: A larger value shows Worldpop-estimated population is higher than census-based population, and vice versa.

False negative rate is the probability that pixels classified as non-urban according to HSR are classified as urban according to GUF (the dataset used to derive the cross-sectional urban patch metrics). The measure was computed using the 2015 data. The false negative rate varies from 0 to 100. Missing values occurred for units that did not have negatives, false positives, true positives, or true negatives (because of missing data, for example) and which had zeroes in the nominator or denominator when computing the rates. Interpretation: Higher values mean a greater probability that non-urban areas per HSR to be classified as urban per GUF.

False positive rate is defined as probability of overlap between urban HSR pixels with non-urban GUF pixels (the dataset used to derive the cross-sectional urban patch metrics) relative to GUF non-urban. In other words, it is the probability that the pixels classified as urban according to HSR are classified as non-urban according to GUF. The measure was computed using the 2015 data. The false positive rate varies from 0 to 100. Missing values occurred for units that did not have negatives, false positives, true positives, or true negatives (because of missing data, for example) and which had zeroes in the nominator or denominator when computing the rates. Interpretation: Higher values mean greater disagreement between HSR and GUF regarding urban pixels.

Measure the price per gallon. Price per gallon of standard gasoline in USD per lite. Interpretation: Price per gallon of standard gasoline in USD per liter. The Gini Index is a widely used summary measure of economic inequality that describes the distribution of wealth or income in a population. The final index calculated ranges from 0 to 1 with 0 expressing perfect equality and 1 expressing perfect inequality. 
Some features of the Gini Index as a measure of inequality are: 1)Population independence: The Gini Index does not depend on the size of the population. However, age structure and population mobility may play a role (people generally have low income when they are younger vs. when they are older); 2) Scale independence: The Gini Index does not depend on the size of the economy. However, it is important to keep in mind that small populations or less diverse economies tend to have small Gini Indices; 3) Transfer principle: if income is transferred from a rich person to a poor person the resulting distribution is more equal. The Gini index was calculated based on per capita household income deciles using disaggregated data on monetary income from salaries, rents, capital, transfers, and other from country household surveys. Data were harmonized across surveys to ensure internal consistency and for comparison between countries and cities, including adjusting per capita incomes for purchasing power parity using 2005 as the reference year and the consumer price index of a given survey year. The primary estimates were completed by the Division of Social Development of CEPAL and verified by the Global Urban Observatory of the UN Habitat.

A summary measure of economic inequality in terms of the distribution of per capita household income in the defined geographic area. The Gini Index is a widely used summary measure of economic inequality that describes distribution of wealth or income in a population. The Gini Index is based on the Lorenz curve, which plots the cumulative percentage of households (from the poorest to the richest) on the horizontal axis against the cumulative percentage of the income or consumption variable on the vertical axis. The Gini Index is calculated as twice the area between the Lorenz curve and the diagonal line crossing the intersection between the horizontal and vertical axes. The final index calculated ranges from 0 to 1 with 0 expressing perfect equality and 1 expressing perfect inequality. Some features of the Gini Index as a measure of inequality are:  
• Population independence: The Gini Index does not depend on the size of the population. However, age structure and population mobility may play a role (people generally have low income when they are younger vs. when they are older) 
• Scale independence: The Gini Index does not depend on the size of the economy. However, it is important to keep in mind that small populations or less diverse economies tend to have small Gini Indi-ces. 
• Transfer principle: if income is transferred from a rich person to a poor person the resulting distribution is more equal.

A summary measure of economic inequality in terms of the distribution of per capita household consumption in the defined geographic area. The Gini Index is a widely used summary measure of economic inequality that describes distribution of wealth or income in a population. The Gini Index is based on the Lorenz curve, which plots the cumulative percentage of households (from the poorest to the richest) on the horizontal axis against the cumulative percentage of the income or consumption variable on the vertical axis. The Gini Index is calculated as twice the area between the Lorenz curve and the diagonal line crossing the intersection between the horizontal and vertical axes. The final index calculated ranges from 0 to 1 with 0 expressing perfect equality and 1 expressing perfect inequality. Some features of the Gini Index as a measure of inequality are:  
• Population independence: The Gini Index does not depend on the size of the population. However, age structure and population mobility may play a role (people generally have low income when they are younger vs. when they are older) 
• Scale independence: The Gini Index does not depend on the size of the economy. However, it is important to keep in mind that small populations or less diverse economies tend to have small Gini Indi-ces. 
• Transfer principle: if income is transferred from a rich person to a poor person the resulting distribution is more equal.

Captures factors related to poverty and general living conditions. This score includes three variables: (1) the percentage of household with piped water inside the dwelling as a marker of living conditions; (2) the percentage of households with overcrowding (defined as more than 3 people per room, excluding kitchen and bathroom); and (3) the percentage of population aged 15-17 attending school. The latter variable is included because low school attendance among adolescents has been linked to poverty and early participation in the labor market, as well as exclusion from productive systems.  The score was created by summing the Z-scores for each component variable. Z-scores were created based on the distributions of all cities (L1AD) or all sub-cities (L2). For the construction of the score, we reverse coded the overcrowding indicator so higher score values signify better living conditions and lower poverty levels.

Refers to services that cities provide to dwellings. This score includes two variables: (1) the percentage of households with access to water source from a municipal public or private water network, and (2) the percentage of households with sewage system connected to a municipal public or private sewage network. The score was created by summing the Z-scores for each variable. Z-scores were created based on the distributions of all cities (L1AD) or all sub-cities (L2). Higher score values signify better service provision in cities.

Refers to educational achievement in the overall population. We used aggregated data from individual level of education to retrieve (1) the percentage of population age 25 or above that has completed high school level or above, and (2) the percentage of population age 25 or above that completed university level or above. The score was created by summing the Z-scores for each variable. Z-scores were created based on the distributions of all cities (L1AD) or all sub-cities (L2). Higher score values signify better educational achievement in the population.

This index aims to summarize the domains of education, water acces, sanitation and overcrowding. For its construction, one measure from each of the four domains of education (proportion of the population aged 25 or older who completed primary education or above), water access (proportion of households with piped water access inside the dwelling), sanitation (proportion of households connected to a public sewage network), and overcrowding (proportion of households with more than 3 people per room) was selected. Each measure was transformed into a Z-score using the mean and standard deviation from the census data. Overcrowding was reverse coded such that the direction of all measures indicate a better social environment. The four measures were summed then divided by 4 assuming equal weights for all four measures.  This index was developed using data for cities (L1AD), the same method was applied to create the index at sub-city (L2) level. The higher the index the best social environment.

Diabetes diagnosis is considered as self-reporting a diagnosis from doctor, physician or other medical professional. Females who reported that the diabetes was diagnosed only during pregnancy are considered to be diabetic.

Prevalence estimate for depression diagnosis in adults aged 18 and older. A survey respondent is classified as having depression diagnosis if they self-report having been told by a physician or health care provider that they have depression.

var_label: Prevalece of fair or poor self-rated health
var_def: Prevalence estimate for fair or poor self-rated health in adults aged 18 years and older. Self-reported health status was dichotomized as reporting very poor, poor or fair health vs. good, very good, or excellent health.

var_label: Prevalence of current pharmacological treatment for hypertension
var_def: Prevalence estimate for current pharmacological treatment for hypertension in adults aged 18 and older. Pharmalogical treatment is defined as self-reporting medication use for hypertension or high blood pressure.

var_label: Prevalence of receiving mammogram in past 2 years amongst women aged 50-79
var_def: Prevalence estimate for receiving a mammogram in past 2 years amongst women aged 50-19.

var_label: Prevalence of meeting recommended physical activity through global physical activity
var_def: Prevalence estimate of meeting WHO exercise guidelines through global physical activity in adults aged 18 and older. A cutoff point of 150 minutes per week was used to classify subjects as active versus inactive in accordance with the recommendations from WHO, 2018 definition of active as at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity throughout the week, or at least 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity throughout the week, or an equivalent combination of moderate- and vigorous-intensity activity. Global physical activity includes physical activity from transportation or leisure time activities.

var_label: Prevalence of meeting recommended physical activity through leisure physical activity
var_def: Prevalence estimate of meeting WHO exercise guidelines through leisure time physical activity in adults aged 18 and older. A cutoff point of 150 minutes per week was used to classify subjects as active versus inactive in accordance with the recommendations from WHO, 2018 definition of active as at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity throughout the week, or at least 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity throughout the week, or an equivalent combination of moderate- and vigorous-intensity activity.

var_label: Prevalence of receiving pap test in past 3 years amongst women aged 25-49
var_def: Prevalence of receiving pap test in past 3 years amongst women aged 25-49.  Three years was chosen to meet the recommended time frame of cancer screening guidelines.

var_label: Major depressive symptoms prevalence based on PHQ-9
var_def: Prevalence Estimate for major depressive symptoms based on Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ9) depressive symptoms scale in adults aged 18 and older. Major depressive symptoms is defined as PHQ9 score >=10.

Prevalence estimate for current smoker amonst adults aged 18 and older. Current smokers are smokers of cigarettes or tobacco products. If a tobacco use question is available, then it is used to create this variable (this follows WHO definitions). If it is absent but a cigarette use question is available, the cigarette use question is used. For CO-ENSIN2010, GT-DHS2015, NI-CAMID2003 and PE-ENDES2016 where lifetime smoking is not available, this uses the version of current smoking available for that survey. NI-CAMDI2003 is current tobacco use > 100 and CO-ENSIN2010, GT-DHS2015, and PE-ENDES2016 are current cigarette use any amount. Recommendations: For most analyses, the combined version of cigarette and tobacco use (SVYSMKHX and SVYSMKCUR) can be used. Caution should be taken in the interpretation given the differences in how tobacco use is collected.

var_label: Prevalence estimate for percent of children who are overweight
var_def: Prevalence estimate for percent of children aged 1-4 years who are overweight. Overweight is defined as weight for height z-score > 2.

var_label: Prevalence estimate for percent of children who are stunting
var_def: Prevalence estimate for percent of children aged 1-4 years who are stunting. Stunting is defined as height for age z-score < -2.

var_label: Prevalence estimate for percent of children who are wasting
var_def: Prevalence estimate for percent of children aged 1-4 years who are wasting. Wasting is defined as weight for height z-score < -2.

This measure was adapted from the Gender Inequality Index developed by the United Nations Development Fund (UNDP), which uses country-level data to characterize three dimensions: health (maternal mortality and adolescent birth rates), empowerment (education and government), and the labor market (labor force participation). This index is a measure of the loss in potential human development due to inequality between women and men in these three dimensions. It ranges from 0, indicating a context where women and men fare equally, to 1, indicating a context in which one gender fares poorly compared to the other in all measured dimensions. For SALURBAL cities, we adapted the index to capture gender-based disadvantage and created 2 versions, one including the three dimensions and the other one including only two dimensions: empowerment and the labor market. This is the verion using all three dimentions. It was constructed using city level data from vital registrations and population projections, census: % female and male labor force participation, % female and male population 25+ with at least high school education, and the % women and men in mayoral positions in the government for the period of 2010-2015 obtained from different sources for each country.  To construct the index, we followed the formulas described by UNDP.

var_label: Gender inequality index (GII) without health component
var_def: This measure was adapted from the Gender Inequality Index developed by the United Nations Development Fund (UNDP), which uses country-level data to characterize three dimensions: health (maternal mortality and adolescent birth rates), empowerment (education and government), and the labor market (labor force participation). This index is a measure of the loss in potential human development due to inequality between women and men in these three dimensions. It ranges from 0, indicating a context where women and men fare equally, to 1, indicating a context in which one gender fares poorly compared to the other in all measured dimensions. For SALURBAL cities, we adapted the index to capture gender-based disadvantage and created 2 versions, one including the three dimensions and the other one including only two dimensions: empowerment and the labor market. This is the verion using two dimentions. It was constructed using city level data from vital registrations and population projections, census: % female and male labor force participation, % female and male population 25+ with at least high school education, and the % women and men in mayoral positions in the government for the period of 2010-2015 obtained from different sources for each country.  To construct the index, we followed the formulas described by UNDP.

var_label: Labor Force Women’s Achievement (or women's achievement score 1)
var_def: The variable captures factors related to employment and marriage. This score includes two variables: 1) % of women in the labor force, 2) % women 15-17 married among the female 15-17 population.  For the construction of the score, we reverse coded the marriage indicator so higher score values signify higher achievements. A higher value indicates higher achievement among women. The variable uses census measures: The labor force participation rate among the female population 15 years or above and the proportion of females aged 15-17 who were married among the total female population ages 15 to 17 (reverse coded). Women's achievement scores were derived from a principle components analysis.

var_label: Education Women’s Achievement   (or women's achievement score 2)
var_def: The variable captures factors related to women’s education. It includes 2 indicators: 1) % women ages 25+ with at least high school education (Proportion of the female population aged 25 or older who completed secondary education or above), 2) % women ages 25+ with at least university education (Proportion of the female population aged 25 or older who completed university education or above). A higher value indicates higher education among women. This version of Education Woman’s Achievement includes all L1ADs where census measures are available and the z-scores are created using the mean and standard deviation of the whole sample. Women's achievement scores were derived from a principle components analysis.

var_label: Health Care Women’s Achievement (or women's achievement score 3)
var_def: The variable refers to health care for women. This score is only available for a limited number of countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and Mexico). We estimated the prevalence of women ages 25 to 49 with a pap test in the last 3 years and the prevalence of women 50 to 49 with a mammogram in the last 2 years. These measures were used as indicators for health care for women.  A higher value indicates better health care among women. Women's achievement scores were derived from a principle components analysis.

var_label: Labor Force Women’s achievement with health care indictors
var_def: The variable captures factors related to employment, marriage, and health care indicators. This score includes four variables: 1) % of women in the labor force, 2) % women 15-17 married among the female 15-17 population, 3) % women 25 to 49 with a pap test in the last 3 years, and 4) % women 50 to 79 with a mammogram in the last 2 years. For the construction of the score, we reverse coded the marriage indicator so higher score values signify higher achievements. A higher value indicates higher achievement. This score is available in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and Mexico. Women's achievement scores were derived from a principle components analysis.

var_label: Education Women’s achievement excluding countries without health care data
var_def: the variable captures factors related to women’s education standardized only to the countries where health care indicators are available. It includes 2 indicators: 1) % women ages 25+ with at least high school education, 2) % women ages 25+ with at least university education. This version uses the same variables as the Woman’s Achievements score 2 (CNSWA2L1AD) with the only difference being that this version creates Z scores for the score components using only the countries with health care data (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and Mexico). This variable is created by standardizing education variables to the distribution of the L1ADs with health care measures available. Women's achievement scores were derived from a principle components analysis.

var_label: Women’s empowerment score 1- Labor force participation
var_def: The variable refers to women’s participation in the labor force depicting some aspect of women’s socio-economic position.  Since it includes the relation of female to male in educational attainment and in labor force participation, it is also accounting for gender inequalities in education and labor market that have been described as relevant in low- and middle-income countries.It includes the following indicators: ratio female/ male in population aged 25 and over with high school level or above; ratio female/ male in population aged 25 or above with complete university or above; labor force participation among women; and ratio female/male in labor force participation. Higher score values signify greater participation of women in labor force and greater education of women relative to men. Women's empowerment scores were derived from a principle components analysis.

This variable refers to the level of educational attainment among women and was used as a measure of differences within women. It includes: % female population with at least complete high school among female population aged 25 years or above; and % of female population with complete university or above among female population aged 25 years or above. Higher score values signify greater education achievement among women. Women's empowerment scores were derived from a principle components analysis.

Respondents are classified as current smokers where they have smoked 100 cigarettes in his or her lifetime and who currently smokes cigarettes.
Respondents are classified as current smokers where they have smoked any amount of cigarettes in his or her lifetime and who currently smokes cigarettes.

Lifetime cigarette use (100+ or 5 packs). Respondents are classified as never, former or current smokers of at least 100 cigarettes or 5 packs of cigarettes. This variable is defined using the United States Center for Disease Control (CDC) definition: current smoker is “an adult who has smoked 100 cigarettes in his or her life-time and who currently smokes cigarettes;” former smoker is “an adult who has smoked at least 100 cigarettes in his or her lifetime but who had quit smoking at the time of interview;” never smoker is “an adult who has never smoked, or who has smoked less than 100 cigarettes in his or her lifetime.”

Lifetime cigarette use (any amount). Respondents are classified as never, former or current smokers (the number of cigarettes is not used). Smoking status is classified as never smokers, former smokers, and current smokers.  A survey participant is classified as never smoker if they report never smoking any cigarettes. Those who have used cigarettes before, but do not currently smoke are considered former smokers. Current smokers are those who have reported smoking cigarettes in their lifetime and are current cigarette smokers.

Overcrowding with more than 3 people per room (excluding kitchen and bathrooms).

Current alcohol use as defined as drinking at least one alcoholic beverage in the past 12 months. This version is referred to as current alcohol use version 2 (V2).

We limited the age range to 18-49 because almost all of the surveys with pregnancy history only ask the questions amongst females in this age range.

Women who report that a diabetes diagnosis was made during pregnancy are classified as NOT having diabetes. This is referred to as Diabetes V1.

A survey participant is classified as having diabetes (diabetes mellitus or gestational diabetes) if they report having been told by a physician or health care provider that they have diabetes or high blood sugar levels, including women who report that this diagnosis was made during pregnancy. This is referred to as Diabetes V2.

A diabetic is defined as receiving any pharmacological treatment if they report using insulin or medications “to lower sugar” or control diabetes prescribed by a health care provider. Those not receiving treatments are considered to not be receiving any pharmacological treatment for depression. The universe is respondents for whom doctor diagnosis of depression is “yes."

Respondent’s education was harmonized using the Integrated Public Use Microdata Series (IPUMS) harmonization definitions representing the highest level of education completed. “Less than Primary” includes those with no education completed and those with less than primary education completed. “Primary” includes those who completed primary education, but with incomplete secondary education. “Secondary” includes those who completed secondary education, those who completed post-secondary education that was not at a university (e.g., technical school), and those who initiated university education but did not complete their university education. “University or higher” includes those who completed a university degree and those who completed more than a university degree, including those with incomplete graduate studies. Graduate studies cannot be distinguished across all countries since not every country asks respondents about any post-university studies (post university is the term sometimes used for masters and doctoral degrees in some countries of the region).

The ever pregnant variable indicates whether adult female respondents indicate that they have ever been pregnant. Pregnancies include all pregnancies including pregnancies that did not come to full term such as premature birth, miscarriage, stillborn, and/or abortion. The universe is all female adults ages 18-49. We limited the age range to 18-49 because almost all of the surveys with pregnancy history only ask the questions amongst females in this age range.

var_label: Fruit Consumption Days Per Week V1
var_def: Number of days per week that fruit is consumed. This will be referred to as Version 1 (V1). For Mexico ENSANUT surveys that have the Food Frequency Questionnaire, this variable is the number of days per week that the fruit of highest intake is consumed (this variable was created selecting the fruit of highest intake in each individual and using the answer “number of days per week” of this specific fruit as a proxy of individual fruit intake). In these cases, this variable can be interpreted as a proxy of the most frequent number of days of fruit consumption.

var_label: Fruit Consumption Days Per Week V2
var_def: Number of days per week that fruit is consumed as the sum of the number of days for all fruits where fruit consumption is assessed with more than one question. This variable was created by summing the number of days for each fruit on the Food Frequency Questionnaire questions together. NOTE: this version is NOT capped. There may be values greater than 7 days. In these cases, this variable can overestimate the number of days for consumption of fruit because it is not possible to guarantee that each day in the summing is a different day of the week. This will be referred to as Version 2

var_label: Fruit Consumption Days Per Week V3
var_def: Number of days per week that fruit is consumed as the sum of the number of days for all fruits where fruit consumption is assessed with more than one question from Food Frequency Questionnaires, capped at 7 days. In these cases, this variable can overestimate the number of days for consumption of fruit because it is not possible to guarantee that each day in the summing is a different day of the week. This will be referred to as Version 3.

var_label: Fruit Servings Per Day V1 (no outliers)
var_def: Average number of servings of fruit per day that an individual consumes in a typical week, using in the formula [Days per week*Servings per day]/7. For surveys that have the Food Frequency Questionnaire, the average number of servings of fruit per day is calculated using the formula above for each fruit separately and the maximum is used. For Chile ENS (2010), this version excludes outlier values greater than 23 servings per day. This will be referred to as Version 1.

var_label: Fruit Servings Per Day V1 (with outliers)
var_def: Average number of servings of fruit per day that an individual consumes in a typical week, using in the formula [Days per week*Servings per day]/7. For surveys that have the Food Frequency Questionnaire, the average number of servings of fruit per day is calculated using the formula above for each fruit separately and the maximum is used. For Chile ENS (2010), this version includes outlier values greater than 23 servings per day. This will be referred to as Version 1a.

Average number of servings of fruit per day that an individual consumes in a typical week considering all fruits together where fruit consumption is assessed with more than one question. This version is available for surveys that have the FFQ (Mexico). This variable was created using the formula above for each fruit separately and summing all fruits together. This will be referred to as Version 2.

var_label: Adequate Fruit and Vegetable Intake V1
var_def: Indicator of adequate daily fruit and vegetable consumption (≥ 5 servings) based on WHO recommendation using number of servings per day version 1 (SVYFVGSVDY1) where 1=adequate (≥ 5) and 0=inadequate (<5). This will be referred to as Version 1.

var_label: Adequate Fruit and Vegetable Intake V2
var_def: Indicator of adequate daily fruit and vegetable consumption (≥ 5 servings) based on WHO recommendation using number of fruit and vegetable servings per day version 2 This version is available for surveys that have the Food Frequency Questionnaire (Mexico). This will be referred to as Version 2.

var_label: Fruit and Vegetable Consumption Days per Week V1
var_def: Number of days per week that fruits and vegetables are consumed, capped at 7 days. Sum of fruits and vegetables version 1 measures and caps at 7 days. For surveys that have the Food Frequency Questionnaire (Mexico) and where the food screeners ask about cooked versus raw vegetables as separate questions (Brazil, Colombia), this variable will be the number of days per week that the fruit and vegetables of highest intake is consumed, capped at 7 days. In these cases, this variable can be interpreted as a proxy of the most frequent number of days of fruit and vegetable consumption. This will be referred to as Version 1.

var_label: Fruit and Vegetable Consumption Days per Week V2
var_def: Number of days per week that fruits and vegetables are consumed as the sum of the number of days for all fruits and vegetables where fruit and/or vegetable consumption is assessed with more than one question for either fruits or vegetables (such as the FFQ). This version is available for surveys that have the Food Frequency Questionnaire and where the food screeners ask about cooked versus raw vegetables as separate questions (Brazil, Colombia). NOTE: this version is NOT capped. There may be values greater than 7 days. In these cases, this variable can overestimate the number of days for consumption of fruit and vegetables because it is not possible to guarantee that each day in the summing is a different day of the week. This will be referred to as Version 2.

var_label: Fruit and Vegetable Consumption Days per Week V3
var_def: Number of days per week that fruits and vegetables are consumed as the sum of the number of days for all fruits and vegetables where fruit and/or vegetable consumption is assessed with more than one question for either fruits or vegetables (such as the FFQ), capped at 7 days. This version is available for surveys that has the Food Frequency Questionnaire (Mexico) and where the food screeners ask about cooked versus raw vegetables as separate questions (Brazil, Colombia). This variable can overestimate the number of days for consumption of fruit and vegetables because it is not possible to guarantee that each day in the summing is a different day of the week. This will be referred to as Version 3.

var_label: Fruit and Vegetable Servings Per Day V1
var_def: Average number of servings of fruits and vegetables per day that an individual consumes in a typical week. This sums together variables SVYFRUSVDY1 and SVYVEGSVDY1. For surveys that have the Food Frequency Questionnaire (Mexico) and for surveys that ask about cooked versus raw vegetables as separate questions (Brazil, Colombia), the average number of servings of vegetables per day is calculated using each vegetables separately and the maximum is used for this version. This will be referred to as Version 1.

var_label: Fruit and Vegetable Servings Per Day V2
var_def: Average number of servings of fruits and vegetables per day that an individual consumes in a typical week considering all fruits and vegetables together where fruit and/or vegetable consumption is assessed with more than one question. For surveys with Food Frequency Questionnaire (Mexico) this version sums together the number of fruits per day and the number vegetables per day. This will be referred to as Version 2.

Hypertension control is defined as persons currently using hypertension medication AND systolic blood pressure<140 AND diastolic blood pressure<90.  Uncontrolled hypertension is defined as persons currently using hypertension medication AND [systolic blood pressure ≥ 140 OR diastolic blood pressure ≥ 90]. Hypertension control is only defined amongst respondents who answered “yes” to using hypertension medications. Hypertension control (SVYHTCTRL) should only be used when the research question is specifi-cally about hypertension control. It SHOULD NOT be used to assess hypertension prevalence.

Presence of hypertension diagnosis by a health care provider among all adults, where adult fe-male respondents who report a hypertension diagnosis during pregnancy are considered to be non-hypertensive. A survey participant is classified as having hypertension if they report having been told by a physician or health care provider that they have high blood pressure or hyperten-sion. This is referred to as Hypertension version 1 (V1).

Presence of hypertension diagnosis by a health care provider among adults regardless of whether hypertension was diagnosed during pregnancy or not (adult female respondents who report a hypertension diagnosis during pregnancy are considered to be hypertensive). A survey participant is classified as having hypertension (hypertension or hypertension during pregnancy) if they report having been told by a physician or health care provider that they have hypertension or high blood pressure. This is referred to as Hypertension version 2 (V2).
Hypertension status defined as hypertension medication use OR systolic blood pressure ≥ 140 OR diastolic blood pressure ≥ 90. This is referred to as Hypertension version (V4).

A participant is defined as hypertensive if they report that a physician told them that they had hypertension AND if they report using medications “to lower blood pressure” or control hyperten-sion prescribed by a health care provider. We include self-reported hypertension by a physician because in all surveys except Chile ENS (2010, 2017) medication use is only asked of those who answer “yes” to self-reported physician diagnosis of hypertension. Therefore, we condition on self-report to align the Chile ENS definition with the definition used in other surveys (in which medication use is only asked among those who self-report physician diagnosed hypertension). Participants are deemed not hypertensive under this definition if they report “NO” to physician diagnosed hypertension or report YES to physician diagnosed hypertension but NO to medica-tion use. This is referred to as Hypertension version 3 (V3).
Indigenous specific to Chile.
Indigenous identification based on self-report.

Self-reported sex of respondent. A survey participant is defined as male if they have a response of “varón,” “masculine,” or “hom-bre.” A survey participant is defined as female if they have a response of “mujer” or “femenino.”

Defined as at least one mammography in the past two years. Two years was chosen due to most countries, except Peru, having no frequency guidelines. Only available amongst females. Mammography is the radiological inspection of the breast tissue looking for agglomeration of calcified tissue which, depending on the pattern, could be suggestive of early stages of malignant tissue transformation that could turn with time into breast cancer. This intervention is extensively available in low-complex health care services, easily to perform by health practitioners, and targeted to all women within a certain age. Thus, measures on coverage of mammogram tests are frequently used as an indicator of accessibility to preventive resources within women’s population.

Defined as at least one mammogram received at any time in the woman’s life. Only available amongst females. Mammography is the radiological inspection of the breast tissue looking for agglomeration of calcified tissue which, depending on the pattern, could be suggestive of early stages of malignant tissue transformation that could turn with time into breast cancer. This intervention is extensively available in low-complex health care services, easily to perform by health practitioners, and targeted to all women within a certain age. Thus, measures on coverage of mammogram tests are frequently used as an indicator of accessibility to preventive resources within women’s population.

Car ownership. Survey participants are classified as owning a car if they or someone in their household reports owning at least one car.

Continuous variable for global physical activity expressed as the number of minutes per week WITH truncation for implausible values. This is computed as the sum of minutes/week of walking (leisure or transport or undifferentiated) and moderate activity and twice the minutes/week of vigorous activity (leisure or work or undifferentiated). Defined as having received a pap test in the past three years. Only available amongst females. Three years was chosen due to most countries, except Peru, having country guidelines that women should be tested every 3 years. The Pap test (or smear) is a screening test used to detect changes in the cells of the cervix that might become cervical cancer, through the examination of cervical cells under microscopy. This intervention is extensively available in low-complex health care services, easily to perform by health practitioners, and targeted to all women within a certain age. Thus, measures on coverage of PAP smear tests are frequently used as an indicator of accessibility to preventive resources within women’s population.

Number of days per week sugar sweetened beverages (SSB) are consumed. For surveys where more than one question related to SSB intake are available, this variable is the number of days per week that the SSB of highest intake is consumed (this variable will be created selecting the SSB of highest intake in each individual). In these cases, this variable can be interpreted as a proxy of the most frequent number of days of SSB consumption. This will be referred to as Version 1.

Number of days per week sugar sweetened beverages (SSB) are consumed. This version is available for surveys where more than one question related to SSB intake is asked. This variable was created summing the questions together. NOTE: this version is NOT capped. There may be values greater than 7 days. In these cases, this variable can overestimate the number of days for consumption of SSB because it is not possible to guarantee that each day in the summing is a different day of the week. This will be referred to as Version 2.

Number of days per week sugar sweetened beverages are consumed. This variable was created summing the questions together and capped at 7 days.
This version is available for surveys where two or more questions related to SSB intake were asked. This variable was created by using the created variable SSB Version 2 and capping at 7 days. In these cases, this variable can overestimate the number of days for consumption of SSB because it is not possible to guarantee that each day in the summing is a different day of the week. This will be referred to as Version 3.

Average number of sugar-sweetened beverages (SSB) per day that an individual consumes in a typical week, using in the formula: [Days per week*Servings per day]/7. For surveys where two or more questions related to SSB intake were assessed the average number of servings of SSB per day is calculated using the formula above for each SSB separately and the maximum is used for this version. This will be referred to as Version 1. For Chile ENS (2017), this version excludes outlier values greater than 36 servings per day.

Child’s education was harmonized using the Integrated Public Use Microdata Series (IPUMS) harmonization definitions representing the highest level of education completed. “Less than Primary” includes those with no education completed and those with less than primary education completed. “Primary” includes those who completed primary education, but with incomplete secondary education. “Secondary” includes those who completed secondary education, those who completed post-secondary education that was not at a university (e.g., technical school), and those who initiated university education but did not complete their university education. “University or higher” includes those who completed a university degree and those who completed more than a university degree, including those with incomplete graduate studies. Graduate studies cannot be distinguished across all countries since not every country asks respondents about any post-university studies (post university is the term sometimes used for masters and doctoral degrees in some countries of the region).

Weight-for-age z-score reflects body weight relative to the child’s age. This indicator can identify whether a child is underweight or severely underweight, but it is not used to classify a child as overweight or obese. This measure can be used to identify is children with low weight-for-height who may be wasted or severely wasted as well as identify children with high weight-for-length/height who may be at risk of becoming overweight or obese. This measure is available and recommended for children aged 0-60 months. It is not calculated for children aged 5-17.
